nameStory: The 'cigar minnow' gets its nickname from its perfectly cylindrical, torpedo-shaped body that looks remarkably like a slender cigar. This sleek shape makes it a fast swimmer and gives it that distinctive profile that's easy to spot underwater. It's also called the 'round scad' because of this same circular cross-section when viewed head-on.
description: The cigar minnow is a small, streamlined fish with a perfectly cylindrical body that tapers at both ends like a torpedo. These silvery fish are built for speed, with their smooth, almost metallic appearance catching light as they move through the water. They're typically small baitfish-sized, rarely exceeding a few inches in length. Though they're members of the jack family, they lack the deep, compressed body shape of their larger relatives.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Perfectly cylindrical, cigar-shaped body that feels firm and streamlined when handled, with a circular cross-section that's the same width from head to tail

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery sides with a metallic sheen that reflects light like polished chrome, often with a slightly darker back and pale belly

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small, pointed fins that fold neatly against the body; tail fin is deeply forked and feels stiff to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small baitfish typically 3-6 inches long, fitting comfortably in your palm with a surprisingly solid, muscular feel for their size

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth positioned at the tip of the pointed head, designed for picking small prey from the water column

habitat: In New England waters, cigar minnows are occasional visitors to offshore areas and deeper coastal waters. They prefer open ocean environments rather than shallow bays or estuaries, typically staying in deeper water columns where they can form schools. When spotted in New England, they're usually found in warmer water masses or during periods when Gulf Stream currents bring tropical species northward.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cool for this warm-water species.
seasonality.summer: Most likely to appear in late summer when water temperatures peak and warm currents may carry them north from southern waters.
seasonality.fall: May occasionally be found in early fall if warm conditions persist, but become increasingly rare as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters during winter months due to cold temperatures.

funFact: Despite being called a 'minnow,' cigar minnows are actually members of the jack family - the same group that includes massive amberjacks and pompanos that can weigh over 100 pounds, making this tiny torpedo one of the smallest members of a family known for producing ocean giants!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small herring or other silvery baitfish, but the cigar minnow's perfectly round, cigar-shaped body is distinctive - if you can roll it like a pencil between your fingers, you've probably got a cigar minnow rather than the flatter herring.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'round scad' might confuse some anglers since most scads are larger fish, but this species represents the smaller end of the scad group. Also, despite being called a 'minnow,' it's not related to true freshwater minnows but gets the name simply due to its small size.
compareHints: As the only Decapterus species regularly found in New England waters, compare it to other small jacks like juvenile blue runners, which have more compressed (flattened) bodies rather than the cigar minnow's distinctive round cross-section. Unlike other jack family members that develop deeper, more diamond-shaped bodies as they grow, cigar minnows maintain their cylindrical torpedo shape throughout their lives.
